learn.title: Solar Inverters: String vs Micro vs Hybrid
learn.intro: Solar panels produce DC electricity, but homes and grids run on AC. Inverters perform this conversion, making them the brain of every PV system. Choosing the right inverter type directly impacts efficiency, cost, and resilience — especially on complex rooftops.
learn.c1_text: String inverters connect a series of panels (a 'string') to one central inverter. They're the cheapest option, typically costing around $1,000 for a 5 kW home system. Like Christmas lights, if one panel underperforms due to shade, the whole string's output drops slightly.
learn.c2_text: Microinverters attach to each individual panel, converting DC to AC right at the module. This panel-level optimization recovers up to 25% more energy on shaded roofs. They cost more upfront but offer superior monitoring and 25-year warranties matching panel lifespans.
learn.c3_text: Hybrid inverters integrate solar and battery management into one unit, reducing equipment costs by 20-30%. India now mandates hybrid-ready inverters for many new commercial installations. They're ideal for the growing rooftop solar-plus-storage market across Indian cities and industrial parks.
learn.stat1: Global PV inverter market reached $12.6 billion in 2024
learn.stat2: String inverters power approximately 70% of utility-scale solar globally
learn.stat3: Microinverters can boost shaded array output by 5-25%
learn.stat4: India installed 4.5 GW of rooftop solar in 2023, mostly string inverter-based

learn.title: Floating Solar Farms: Power on Water
learn.intro: Floating photovoltaic (FPV) systems install solar panels on reservoirs, lakes, and ponds. With land becoming scarce for utility-scale projects, water-based solar offers a clever solution that also reduces evaporation — a critical benefit in drought-prone regions.
learn.c1_text: Floating panels shade water surfaces, reducing evaporation by up to 70%. A typical 1 MW FPV system saves roughly 5 million liters of water annually. Think of it as a giant solar parasol that generates electricity while shielding precious water from the sun.
learn.c2_text: Water keeps panels cooler than land, improving efficiency by 10-15%. PV cells lose about 0.5% efficiency per degree Celsius above 25°C. On hot Indian afternoons when land temperatures exceed 45°C, floating systems can outperform ground-mounted equivalents significantly.
learn.c3_text: India's largest floating solar plant at Omkareshwar Dam in Madhya Pradesh generates 600 MW, one of the world's biggest. The Ministry of New and Renewable Energy targets 10 GW of floating solar by 2026, leveraging the country's vast reservoir infrastructure across states.
learn.stat1: Global FPV capacity grew from 1 MW to 6.2 GW between 2013 and 2023
learn.stat2: FPV systems reduce water evaporation by 50-70% depending on climate
learn.stat3: Cooling effect boosts panel efficiency by 10-15% versus land installations

learn.title: Climate Finance and COP Agreements
learn.intro: Each year, nations gather at the Conference of the Parties (COP) to negotiate climate action. For developing countries, these agreements determine access to billions in funding needed to leapfrog fossil fuels and build resilient, low-carbon energy infrastructure.
learn.c1_text: At COP2009, developed nations promised $100 billion annually to developing countries for climate action. This target was only formally met in 2022, with much arriving as loans rather than grants. Think of it as a down payment on a much larger transition bill.
learn.c2_text: At COP27 in Egypt, nations agreed to establish a Loss and Damage Fund helping vulnerable countries recover from climate disasters. Initial pledges reached $700 million. Critics argue this is symbolic — the International Energy Agency estimates needs exceed $2 trillion annually by 2030.
learn.c3_text: India requires $10 trillion by 2070 to achieve net-zero, according to government estimates. The Green Climate Fund has approved projects worth $2.5 billion in India. At COP28, India launched the Global Biofuels Alliance, positioning itself as a leader in sustainable fuel transitions.

learn.title: India's Green Hydrogen Mission Explained
learn.intro: Green hydrogen, produced by splitting water using renewable electricity, could replace fossil fuels in steel, fertilizer, and heavy transport. India's National Green Hydrogen Mission launched in 2023 positions it as a global manufacturing hub for this emerging fuel.
learn.c1_text: India targets 5 million metric tonnes of green hydrogen production by 2030, requiring approximately 125 GW of dedicated renewable capacity. Think of it as building an entirely new energy carrier from scratch — green hydrogen stores energy that batteries cannot practically hold long-term.
learn.c2_text: The mission offers ₹50 per kg production incentive for three years, capped at ₹250 billion total. Additionally, manufacturers receive 30% capital subsidies for electrolyzer plants. This makes Indian green hydrogen potentially cost-competitive with grey hydrogen by 2028.
learn.c3_text: Priority sectors include steel, refining, fertilizers, and heavy mobility. India imports 85% of its oil and 50% of natural gas — green hydrogen could transform energy security. Reliance Industries plans 100 GW of solar capacity dedicated to hydrogen production by 2030.

learn.title: Iron-Air Batteries for 100+ Hour Storage
learn.intro: Lithium-ion batteries dominate short-duration storage, but grids need multi-day backup. Iron-air batteries use rusting and unrusting chemistry — one of Earth's cheapest materials — to store electricity for 100+ hours, transforming seasonal grid reliability.
learn.c1_text: Iron-air batteries generate electricity by letting iron rust (oxidize). Charging reverses the process, turning rust back into iron. Imagine a battery that 'breathes' oxygen in and out — the air itself is one of the electrodes. Iron costs roughly 20x less than lithium per kWh.
learn.c3_text: India's National Electricity Plan targets 42 GW of battery storage by 2030, much requiring long-duration solutions. Iron-air technology could support India's rural electrification challenges where solar needs to bridge multi-day cloudy periods. State utilities are exploring pilots.

learn.title: LCOE: Comparing Power Sources Fairly
learn.intro: Levelised Cost of Energy (LCOE) measures the lifetime cost per megawatt-hour of electricity, factoring in construction, fuel, operations and decommissioning. It's the universal yardstick letting us compare apples-to-apples between coal, solar, and nuclear.
learn.c1_text: LCOE = (Total Lifecycle Costs) ÷ (Total Lifetime Energy Output). It smooths upfront expenses over 25-40 years. Imagine buying a car: instead of comparing sticker prices, LCOE tells you the per-kilometer cost including fuel and maintenance across the vehicle's life.
learn.c2_text: Utility solar LCOE fell from $378/MWh in 2010 to $44/MWh in 2023 — an 88% decline. Onshore wind dropped 70% over the same period. Meanwhile, new coal averaged $117/MWh. Renewables now beat fossil fuels on cost alone in most sunny, windy regions.
learn.c3_text: India's solar tariffs hit ₹2.50/kWh ($30/MWh) in 2024 auctions — among the world's lowest. However, LCOE excludes grid integration costs of ₹1-2/kWh needed for storage and balancing. MNRE now mandates storage alongside large renewable tenders to capture full system costs.
